facts.claim: The mandate system placed former German and Ottoman territories under administration by other powers, formally under League oversight.
The League of Nations was responsible for supervising the mandate system established after the war.
The League’s mandate system placed territories under administering powers while claiming international oversight; the path to self-government varied.
Former Ottoman territories in the Middle East were assigned to British and French administration under the mandate system.
Mandates remained under external administration and did not grant immediate sovereign independence.
The postwar settlement redrew borders and created mandates, but it did not resolve every national or territorial dispute.
The League was intended to provide a forum for cooperation and collective security after the war.
The U.S. Senate did not ratify the Treaty of Versailles, and the United States never joined the League.
Collective security relied on members acting together against threats to peace, but the League lacked reliable enforcement power.
The League’s structure included an Assembly and a Council, along with a permanent Secretariat.
The League relied on its members for sanctions and enforcement and had no independent military force.
U.S. non-membership weakened the League’s political weight and limited the collective security framework.
Japan announced its withdrawal from the League after the organisation criticised its actions in Manchuria.
The League condemned Japanese actions, but could not compel Japan to withdraw from Manchuria.
The Covenant included commitments concerning members’ territorial integrity and political independence.
The League developed institutions and rules, but political divisions and reliance on member action limited its effectiveness.
The Weimar Constitution was adopted in 1919 and established Germany’s postwar republic.
The Reichstag was the elected national parliament of the Weimar Republic.
Article 48 allowed the president to take emergency measures under specified conditions; its use became politically significant.
Germany experienced severe hyperinflation in 1923, eroding the value of the mark and savings.
The Dawes Plan of 1924 restructured reparations payments and helped stabilise the German economy, with reliance on U.S. loans.
Weimar Germany faced major crises and also achieved periods of recovery; historians do not treat its collapse as inevitable.
The 1919 constitution established a republic with parliamentary institutions and an elected president.
Proportional representation allowed a range of parties to win seats, contributing to coalition politics; it was one factor among several in political instability.
The global economic downturn began after the 1929 crash and spread internationally.
Germany’s mid-1920s recovery relied significantly on foreign credit, making the withdrawal of U.S. loans damaging.
The Depression brought mass unemployment and economic hardship to Germany.
The Depression intensified hardship and helped radical parties gain support, though it was not the only cause of Nazi growth.
The Depression was an important contributing factor, but Nazi growth also reflected earlier developments and political choices.
The downturn spread through international finance and trade, with effects that varied among countries.
Mussolini founded the Fascist movement and was appointed prime minister in October 1922.
The Fascist March on Rome took place in October 1922; King Victor Emmanuel III then appointed Mussolini prime minister.
Hindenburg appointed Hitler chancellor on 30 January 1933.
Hitler led the Nazi Party, which gained support in the political crises of the Weimar era.
Mussolini was the leading figure of Italian Fascism, an authoritarian nationalist movement.
Hitler was appointed chancellor by Hindenburg; the Nazis then consolidated power through political manoeuvres, legislation, coercion and propaganda.
The decree suspended key civil liberties and enabled arrests and repression after the Reichstag fire.
The Enabling Act gave Hitler’s cabinet legislative power, undermining parliamentary government.
The Nazi regime combined legal changes with violence, propaganda and institutional control to destroy opposition.
Hitler’s appointment and subsequent consolidation involved several political and legal steps, supported by coercion and violence.
After January 1933, the Nazi government dismantled democratic institutions and consolidated dictatorial power.
The Nazi regime eliminated meaningful political competition and established a dictatorship.
The Mukden Incident preceded Japan’s occupation and conquest of Manchuria.
The League investigated the crisis and criticised Japan, but lacked the means and unity to reverse the occupation.
Italy invaded Ethiopia in October 1935.
The League condemned the invasion and imposed sanctions, but these measures did not prevent Italy’s conquest.
Foreign states and volunteers became involved on different sides; diplomatic efforts to limit intervention were contested and uneven.
Japan’s expansion in Manchuria and Italy’s invasion of Ethiopia exposed the League’s inability to halt aggression.
German troops re-entered the demilitarised Rhineland in March 1936.
The Anschluss was the annexation of Austria by Nazi Germany in March 1938.
The Munich Agreement of September 1938 allowed Germany to annex the Sudetenland.
British and French leaders made concessions to Hitler’s demands, hoping to preserve peace; the policy did not prevent further expansion.
Germany occupied the rest of the Czech lands in March 1939, showing that the Munich settlement did not end expansion.
Germany remilitarised the Rhineland in 1936, annexed Austria in 1938, gained the Sudetenland at Munich, and occupied the rest of the Czech lands in 1939.
Germany and the Soviet Union signed the pact in August 1939.
The secret protocol divided spheres of influence in Eastern Europe, including provisions concerning Poland.
German forces invaded Poland on 1 September 1939.
Britain and France declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939, after the invasion of Poland.
The pact was signed in August 1939, Germany invaded Poland on 1 September, and Britain and France declared war on 3 September.
Interwar economic crises, authoritarian politics, aggression and weak collective responses combined in the path to war; the process cannot be reduced to one cause.
